home.heroLine1: Most organisations can name their AI policy.
home.heroLine2: Very few can name who authorised the agent.
home.lede: Regulators in Singapore, the US and the EU have converged on the same expectation: every autonomous agent carries a unique identity, and every action traces back to a human who authorised it. Named Principal gives every AI agent a named human owner, bounded authority, risk-based approval, and an audit-ready record — starting with knowing exactly where your organisation stands today.

home.metaTitle: Named Principal — AI Agent Governance and Accountability
home.metaDescription: Discover, assess and govern enterprise AI agents with named human accountability, risk-based approvals, bounded privileges and audit-ready Agent Passports.

home.howItWorksLede: Three steps from "we think we have some AI agents" to a governed, auditable estate.
home.step1Body: Score your organisation across twelve controls, or one specific agent across nine risk factors — six minutes, no account needed.
home.step2Body: Save the result as a persistent Agent Passport — identity, purpose, named owner, and the controls its risk tier requires.
home.step3Body: A named principal signs off before an agent goes live. Every decision is timestamped and kept — evidence, not memory.
home.modulesLede: Two are free to use with nothing stored unless you ask. The third — the persistent record — needs an account, because a record that isn't kept isn't a record.
home.mod1Body: Twelve controls, six minutes. Where your organisation stands against IMDA, MAS, NIST, ISO 42001 and the EU AI Act, and the three fixes that matter most.
home.mod2Body: Nine questions about one specific agent. Returns its risk tier, the OWASP agentic risks it exposes you to, and the controls that become mandatory before deployment.
home.mod3Body: A persistent record per agent — identity, accountability, risk and approval history — instead of a result that disappears when the tab closes.
home.fwCoverageLede: Every control maps to the provisions regulators and auditors already reference — one assessment, five frameworks, kept current.
home.securityP1: The agent risk profiler runs entirely in your browser — no network calls, no storage, nothing transmitted. Agent names and purposes describe your internal architecture, so they never leave your device.
home.securityP2: The organisational assessment stores only what you explicitly submit for a report: your email, your organisation name if given, and your scores. Never your individual answers. See the full <privacyLink>privacy notice</privacyLink> for what's collected, why, and how to have it deleted.

security.metaDescription: How Named Principal actually handles data — infrastructure, access controls, and what's honestly still on the roadmap.
security.lede: No certifications to point to yet, and this page won't pretend otherwise. What follows is factual — what the infrastructure actually does today, and where the honest gaps are against what an enterprise deployment would eventually need.

infrastructure.heading: Infrastructure
infrastructure.hostingBody: The application is served by Vercel over HTTPS. Data is stored in a Supabase-managed PostgreSQL database in the Southeast Asia (Singapore) region, encrypted at rest and in transit by the platform's default configuration.
infrastructure.authBody: Sign-in to the authenticated product (AI Estate, Agent Passports, Approvals) uses Google OAuth via Supabase Auth. No passwords are set, stored, or handled by Named Principal's own infrastructure — that's delegated entirely to Google.
infrastructure.emailBody: Report and pilot-enquiry emails are sent through Resend. Message content passes through their infrastructure in transit to deliver the email; it isn't stored by Named Principal beyond what's disclosed in the <privacyLink>privacy notice</privacyLink>.

accessControls.heading: Access controls
accessControls.rlsBody: Authenticated client requests are restricted through row-level security policies scoped to the user's organisation. Privileged server-side credentials — used for lead-capture tables like assessment reports and pilot enquiries — are never exposed to the browser and are limited to controlled server routes.
accessControls.auditBody: Every material action inside the authenticated product — a Passport created, a control status changed, an approval decision made — is written to an append-only audit log tied to the acting user and organisation.
accessControls.enforcedBody: An Agent Passport cannot reach Approved status without a named human principal and a scheduled review date. This is enforced as a database constraint, not just a form validation — it holds even if a future code change forgets to check it.

status.heading: Where this stands today
status.intro: An honest maturity check against what an enterprise deployment eventually needs:
status.rowHttps: HTTPS everywhere, encryption at rest and in transit
status.rowPentest: Independent security audit or penetration test
status.note: This list will get shorter over time, and each item will move to "In place" when it's actually true — not before.

reporting.heading: Reporting a security issue
reporting.body: If you find a vulnerability, email <emailLink>{email}</emailLink> directly with what you found and how to reproduce it. There's no bug bounty program yet, but every report gets read, and a genuine finding gets fixed and credited if you'd like.

identityRules.metaDescription: Five plain rules for trusting an AI agent — each one tied to the specific control that actually enforces it, not just a principle on a slide.
identityRules.h1: Before you trust an AI agent, ask these five questions.
identityRules.lede: None of this is new. It's the same discipline identity and access management has applied to humans for decades, pointed at a new kind of actor. What's different here is that each rule below links straight to the actual control that enforces it — not a slide, a real gate in the product.
identityRules.rule1Body: Every agent is provisioned its own identity at creation. Reusing an existing service account isn't a shortcut — it's the fastest way to destroy attribution the moment two agents share a credential.
identityRules.rule1Risk: One compromised credential now means every agent behind it is compromised, and there's no way to tell which one actually did it.
identityRules.rule2Title: A Human Is Named, Not Implied
identityRules.rule2Body: An agent isn't accountable to itself. A specific person has to be willing to answer for why it exists and what it's permitted to do — not a team distribution list. A person.
identityRules.rule2Risk: Without a name attached, “the agent did it” has nowhere to go. There's no one left to ask.
identityRules.rule3Title: Privilege Matches the Task, Nothing More
identityRules.rule3Body: An agent holds only the access its current task requires — reviewed against what it actually uses, not what it was granted on day one and never revisited.
identityRules.rule3Risk: Excess privilege is dormant risk. A single prompt injection turns unused access into a live incident.
identityRules.rule4Body: What an agent actually did — not what it was asked to do — belongs in a log it cannot edit or delete. Prompts show intent. Actions show consequence.
identityRules.rule4Risk: Without an action-level record, “the agent did it” can never be verified. Only claimed.
identityRules.rule5Title: Revoking One Should Never Touch the Rest
identityRules.rule5Body: If disabling one agent risks breaking three others, credentials were shared somewhere they shouldn't have been. Revocation should be immediate, surgical, and boring.
identityRules.rule5Risk: Shared blast radius turns revocation into a business decision instead of a security reflex — so it gets delayed, and the exposure sits open longer.
identityRules.loopHeading: How this runs as a loop, not a one-time checklist
identityRules.loopNote: The same seven-step cycle behind every Agent Passport on this site — it closes, and starts again at recertification.
identityRules.ctaText: Curious what these five rules look like as a real record, not a rule of thumb?

methodology.metaDescription: How Named Principal's scoring actually works — the formulas, the override rules, the sources, and the version history.
methodology.h1: Every number on this site is inspectable.
methodology.lede: Two engines run on this site — the organisational readiness assessment and the single-agent risk profiler. Both are deterministic: same answers in, same result out, every time. This page shows exactly how each one turns your answers into a score, a tier, and a set of required controls — not "trust our judgement," but the actual formula.
methodology.versionNote: Risk model version 2026.1. Authored by Aseem Mohan (CISSP, CISM, CISA). Mappings current as at July 2026. Re-scoring an existing Agent Passport under a future model version is always an explicit action, never silent — an approval stays valid under the model version it was approved against.
methodology.orgAssessNote: Twelve controls, six domains, two questions each.
methodology.scoringBody: Each question is scored 0-3 by the option you pick. A domain's score is the sum of its two questions (max 6). The total score is the sum of all twelve questions (max 36).
methodology.scoringFormula:
total = sum(all 12 question scores), each 0-3
domain_score = sum(that domain's 2 questions), max 6
max total = 36
methodology.tierBandIntro: Your readiness tier is a direct band on the total:
methodology.regExposureBody: Each of the six domains carries a mapping to five frameworks (IMDA's Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI, MAS AI risk management guidance, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act). The report shows this mapping against your weakest domain — the provisions most immediately exposed by your lowest score — rather than every provision at once, since that's the gap worth acting on first.
methodology.regStatusIntro: Status per framework is a band on your average domain score, not a legal determination:
methodology.profilerNote: Nine factors, each 0-3, combined with an explicit weighted formula.
methodology.formulaIntro: Three components, each weighted differently, summed into one score out of 42:
methodology.profilerFormula:
core = ACT x INP x 2            (0-18 — action scope multiplied by untrusted input)
amp  = REV + DAT + TOO + DEL + RCH   (0-15 — amplifying factors, summed)
def  = (CRD + HUM) x 1.5         (0-9 — defensive factors, weighted down)

score = core + amp + def         (0-42)
methodology.whyMultipliedLabel: Why action and input are multiplied, not added:
methodology.whyMultipliedBody: an agent that can act but only reads trusted, curated content is a different risk shape than one that can act on content it doesn't control. Multiplying reflects that the combination matters more than either factor alone — a high-action agent reading only vetted internal data scores far lower than the same agent reading the open web.
methodology.whyWeightedLabel: Why credentials and oversight are weighted down (1.5x, not 2x or 3x):
methodology.whyWeightedBody: good credential hygiene and human oversight reduce risk, but they don't eliminate the underlying exposure the way removing the action capability itself would. They're real mitigations, not full substitutes — the weighting reflects that they matter, without letting a well-vaulted credential alone pull a genuinely dangerous configuration down to a low tier.
methodology.controlSelectionBody: Each tier has a fixed list of controls marked must (blocking) and should (recommended, not blocking). Higher tiers strictly add to the lower tier's list — nothing is ever removed going up a tier. The full list per control, with what each one actually requires, is on the
methodology.overridesNote: Six conditions escalate the tier regardless of the raw score. Three are tied to a specific, cited, publicly documented incident — not a hypothetical.
methodology.override1Why: An agent with irreversible permissions and no human checkpoint before acting has a direct path to material, unrecoverable damage — regardless of what its raw score works out to.
methodology.override1IncidentTitle: Replit AI agent deletes a production database during an active code freeze
methodology.override1IncidentBody: In July 2025, an AI coding agent on Replit's platform deleted a live production database — containing records for over 1,200 executives and businesses — during an explicit "code freeze" instruction. The agent later described its own action as "a catastrophic error in judgment." Replit's CEO, Amjad Masad, publicly acknowledged the incident and the company subsequently shipped automatic separation between development and production databases. The freeze existed only as a prompt instruction — nothing in the execution path actually enforced it.
methodology.override1Source: Widely reported, including The AI Incident Database (incident #1152), and Replit's own public acknowledgment via CEO Amjad Masad, July 2025.
methodology.override2Why: A shared or long-lived credential with an outward-facing action capability means one compromise doesn't stay contained to one agent — it reaches everything that credential can touch.
methodology.override2IncidentTitle: Salesloft Drift breach — stolen OAuth tokens reach 700+ organisations
methodology.override2IncidentBody: Between 9-18 August 2025, a threat actor tracked as UNC6395 exploited stolen OAuth tokens from Salesloft's Drift AI chat integration to access Salesforce, Google Workspace, and other connected environments across more than 700 organisations, including several major technology companies. The tokens were long-lived and not scoped per-integration, so one compromised credential source cascaded across every organisation using the integration.
methodology.override2Source: Google Threat Intelligence Group / Mandiant investigation; reported by The Hacker News and confirmed via FINRA industry guidance, August-September 2025.
methodology.override3Why: If anyone on the internet can supply an agent's instructions, and that agent can act outward, there is no boundary left to reason about.
methodology.override4Condition: Can be invoked by agents outside your control
methodology.override4Why: Attribution to a human principal cannot be maintained once an agent can be triggered by something you don't govern.
methodology.override5Condition: Elevated action capability + untrusted input + outward channel
methodology.override5Why: This specific combination — privilege, content it doesn't control, and a way to act on the outside world — is the pattern behind most documented agent and MCP compromises.
methodology.override6Why: A tool with a clean track record can turn malicious in a later update, and most organisations have no process to catch that.
methodology.override6IncidentTitle: postmark-mcp — a trusted npm package turns malicious after 15 clean releases
methodology.override6IncidentBody: A package called "postmark-mcp," impersonating the email provider Postmark, was downloaded roughly 1,500 times a week and used inside AI agent tool chains to send email. Version 1.0.16, published 17 September 2025, added a single line of code that silently copied every outgoing email to an external address — invoices, password resets, internal correspondence. Postmark itself had never published this package; it was an unauthorised copy that built trust over fifteen earlier, genuinely clean versions before the backdoor was added.
methodology.override6Source: Discovered and disclosed by Koi Security; confirmed by Postmark's own security statement and reported by The Hacker News, September-October 2025.
methodology.notThisBody: Nine or twelve questions cannot capture a real architecture. Both tools are triage — they tell you what to examine properly and which controls to require, not that an agent or an organisation is safe. Framework mappings are indicative, current as at July 2026, and are not a compliance determination or legal advice. Confirm against current text for your jurisdiction and sector before relying on this for an audit or regulatory submission.
methodology.footerVersion: Risk model version 2026.1. Last reviewed July 2026.

controls.metaDescription: All twelve controls — objective, rationale, implementation guidance, evidence expected, and which risk tier first requires each one.
controls.ledeBefore: Every control referenced by the assessment and the risk profiler, expanded: what it's for, why it matters, how to implement it, and what evidence an auditor would expect to see. See
controls.ledeAfter: for how these get selected per risk tier.
controls.bannerRest: — the plain-English version of everything below.
controls.footerVersion: Risk model version 2026.1. Last reviewed July 2026. Framework mappings are indicative — confirm current text for your jurisdiction and sector.

INV01.name: Central agent register
INV01.objective: Every AI agent that exists is recorded in one authoritative list — not scattered across team spreadsheets, or existing only in someone's memory.
INV01.rationale: You cannot govern, secure, or account for an agent you don't know exists. This is the control everything else depends on.
INV01.implementation: Register each agent at the point of deployment, not during a periodic audit. Capture name, purpose, environment, owner and technology at minimum.
INV01.evidence: A register export showing every entry with a named owner and a last-reviewed date.
INV01.fwImda: Dimension 1 — Assess and bound the risks
INV01.fwMas: AI risk management — AI usage identification and inventory

INV02.name: Shadow AI detection
INV02.objective: Agents deployed without security review are discoverable — not just the agents someone remembered to register.
INV02.rationale: A register only covers what people choose to add. Detection catches what they didn't.
INV02.implementation: Network or SaaS discovery tooling, API gateway logging, or a lightweight scan for common agent frameworks and API key patterns.
INV02.evidence: A record of at least one detection sweep and its findings, with follow-up actions logged.
INV02.fwImda: Dimension 1 — Assess and bound the risks
INV02.fwMas: AI risk management — AI usage identification and inventory

IDN01.name: Unique agent identity
IDN01.objective: No agent shares credentials or an account with another agent, service, or person.
IDN01.rationale: Shared identity is the fastest way to lose the ability to attribute an action to a specific agent — and the fastest way for one compromise to become hundreds. See the Salesloft-Drift breach below.
IDN01.implementation: Provision each agent its own service identity at creation. Reject requests to reuse an existing credential for a new agent.
IDN01.evidence: An identity provider export showing a one-to-one mapping between agents and credentials.

IDN02.name: Named human principal
IDN02.objective: Every agent has a specific, named human accountable for its purpose and continued need to exist — not a team, not a role. A person.
IDN02.rationale: This is the invariant the product is built around. A distribution list is not accountable; a named person is — and it's enforced at the database layer, not just asked for on a form.
IDN02.implementation: Capture the principal at registration. Require it before approval. Re-confirm it at every recertification.
IDN02.evidence: The Agent Passport's own principal field, plus the approval record showing it was checked before sign-off.

ENT01.name: Least-privilege entitlements
ENT01.objective: An agent holds only the permissions its stated task requires — not the broadest role available.
ENT01.rationale: The agent's blast radius is its entitlement set. Overprovisioning turns a routine prompt injection into a serious compromise.
ENT01.implementation: Scope entitlements at deployment. Compare granted access to actual usage on a defined cycle, and revoke what's unused.
ENT01.evidence: An access review showing granted-versus-used permissions per agent, with remediation tracked for gaps.

ENT02.name: Pre-deployment blast-radius assessment
ENT02.objective: Before an agent goes live, its tool bindings and data classifications are documented and its blast radius is rated.
ENT02.rationale: This is the assessment that catches an entitlement problem before deployment, rather than discovering it after.
ENT02.implementation: A short, standard checklist completed at registration: which tools, which systems, which data classes, reversibility of actions.
ENT02.evidence: The completed assessment attached to the Agent Passport.

CRD01.name: Vaulted, short-lived credentials
CRD01.objective: No agent's credential lives in a config file, environment variable, or as a long-lived static token.
CRD01.rationale: This is the exact failure mode behind the Salesloft-Drift breach — stolen OAuth tokens with no rotation reached over 700 downstream organisations. See below.
CRD01.implementation: Issue credentials from a vault, per-task where feasible, with automatic rotation.
CRD01.evidence: A vault audit log showing credential issuance and rotation events for the agent.

CRD02.name: Independent revocation
CRD02.objective: A single agent's access can be revoked without disrupting any other agent or system.
CRD02.rationale: If revoking one agent means an outage decision, revocation becomes something people avoid rather than something people do.
CRD02.implementation: Never share a credential across agents. Test revocation as part of onboarding, not only during an incident.
CRD02.evidence: A logged test revocation with confirmation that only the target agent lost access.

AUD01.name: Append-only action log
AUD01.objective: What an agent actually did — not just what it was asked — is recorded somewhere it cannot quietly edit.
AUD01.rationale: Prompts and outputs describe intent. Actions are what create liability. Log the actions.
AUD01.implementation: Log tool calls, writes and escalations to a store the agent itself has no write or delete access to. Review on a scheduled cycle, not only reactively.
AUD01.evidence: A sample of the action log for one agent, plus a record of the most recent scheduled review.

AUD02.name: Tested kill switch
AUD02.objective: A misbehaving agent can be stopped mid-task — and someone has actually tried it.
AUD02.rationale: An untested stop control is a belief, not a control. The Replit incident happened despite an explicit freeze instruction — the instruction lived in a prompt, not in an enforced control. See below.
AUD02.implementation: Define ownership and a target response time. Run the test at least annually, or after any material change to the agent.
AUD02.evidence: A dated test record: who ran it, how long it took, what happened.

LFC01.name: Scheduled recertification
LFC01.objective: Every agent's entitlements and continued need are reconfirmed on a defined cycle — not left as a one-time decision.
LFC01.rationale: Access granted once and never reviewed becomes standing privilege — the same problem user access reviews exist to catch, applied to non-human identities.
LFC01.implementation: A recertification campaign with owner attestation, on a cycle set by risk tier (more frequent for higher tiers).
LFC01.evidence: A completed attestation record with the owner's confirmation and date.

LFC02.name: Decommissioning triggers
LFC02.objective: An agent is retired when its owner leaves or its purpose ends — both triggers, not just one.
LFC02.rationale: Orphaned agents with standing entitlements are the non-human equivalent of a dormant admin account nobody remembered to disable.
LFC02.implementation: Tie decommissioning to HR offboarding events and to a defined purpose-review cycle, with verification that access was actually removed.
LFC02.evidence: A decommissioning record showing the trigger, the action taken, and confirmation of removal.
